extracted.intended_audience: Users asking questions on Mathematics Stack Exchange (new and experienced askers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing clear, answerable mathematics questions on Math.SE: how to choose titles, add context, show work, format and tag posts, and follow contest/policy requirements so the community can provide helpful answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for answers before posting
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for answers before posting a question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the site search and read suggested possible duplicates (the system suggests duplicates when you write the title). Checking for existing answers prevents duplicates, cluttering the site, and wasting answerers' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context
rubrics_metrics.description: Context matters: include motivation, where the question comes from, and the intended audience/level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the source (textbook, paper, class, research, random thought), why you care about the question, and what background/notation you expect answerers to assume. This helps responders choose appropriate level, notation, and relevant theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include your work / show attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: Include your attempts and work toward solving the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing computations, partial proofs, or attempted ideas helps others diagnose errors, focus help, and demonstrates you are not using the site as an answer machine. It also often helps you spot the mistake yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'no-clue' questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't post only the problem statement with 'I don't know how to begin'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have no idea, still write definitions, try simple cases, examine examples, try n=1,2,3 or specific matrices/numbers, and state what you tried. Use these starter strategies: write down definitions, try special/smaller cases, list related theorems, and include representative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a good title
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your title descriptive—ideally the question itself—so it conveys the content faithfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the title to communicate the question (not just tags), include the integral/expression via MathJax if helpful, avoid personal pleas in the title, keep vertical space small (some plain words required), and ensure the question body does not depend on the title. Titles can be fairly long (15–150 characters), but be concise and universal rather than personal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical typesetting (MathJax)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use MathJax for TeX-like mathematical typesetting in posts and titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MathJax makes notation readable; consult the MathJax/LaTeX documentation for supported commands. MathJax is supported in titles but follow community guidelines (avoid excessive vertical space). Not every LaTeX command is supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear English, proper spelling/grammar, paragraphs, and Markdown to make the question readable and of lasting value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the actual question stand out (bold or a heading like 'My question'), use paragraphs to avoid dense blocks, avoid putting key parts in images (images are not searchable or accessible), and use proper punctuation. If English is not your first language, consider posting in your native language or asking for translation help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the question visible and self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not force readers to click external links or rely on images/screenshots for the problem statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put all essential content in the post text so it's searchable and accessible to screen readers. If referencing a paper/book include sufficient bibliographic info or a DOI; do not place the core problem inside an image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag your question correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags should describe the mathematical content, not the context in which you encountered the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use up to five tags that reflect the subject area (content) of the question. Use tag wikis to check fit. Avoid meta tags (e.g., soft-question) as primary tags; tags attract experts who follow them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pare the question to its basics
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplify the problem to its core question before asking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove extraneous constants and complexities; ask the simplest representative version (e.g., scale variables, consider simplest nontrivial case). Avoid irrelevant backstory and 'throat clearing' that wastes readers' time. Use simple, non-confusing notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing abbreviations and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit uncommon abbreviations and explain notation that could be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using abbreviations or symbols that aren't universally recognized (or have multiple meanings), define them. For example, clarify 'iff' vs 'if' if there is a chance of misunderstanding. When in doubt, use plain English to explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask one question per post
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit a post to one main question (exceptions: a closely related variation may be acceptable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate distinct questions into separate posts to keep threads focused. Two closely related questions (one a small variation) can sometimes be included, but generally avoid multiple unrelated questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contest questions: state source and follow policy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the question is from a contest or contest training, clearly state the source and whether the contest is ongoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the contest name/date and use the contest-math tag; do not ask for help on current, ongoing contests (cheating policy). Provide context about prior attempts and simpler versions tested to show you are not seeking to cheat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give definitions and full references when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide definitions for nonstandard terms and bibliographic references for cited papers or textbooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term is ambiguous or specialist, either define it or link to a reliable source. For papers cite DOI or full bibliographic information so others can find the source easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check small examples and computational tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Test conjectures or properties on small cases or with computer searches to rule out trivial counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running small examples helps detect mistakes and supplies material to include in the question. If you run code to test examples, include the code or a description of the computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post code or language-universal pseudocode when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: If your question involves computer code or computations, include the code (or clear pseudocode) and outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting runnable code allows others to reproduce results; if language-specific code would be inaccessible to some, provide clear pseudocode or step-by-step descriptions. Code demonstrates effort and aids debugging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid non-descriptive titles and pleas
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use vague or plea-based titles like 'Help me!'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague titles don't inform potential answerers what you need. Use descriptive titles that summarize the problem rather than personal circumstances or requests for help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell us where you are struggling and what you know
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state the point of difficulty and what parts you already understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicating where you are stuck lets answerers target explanations. State known lemmas, partial results, or false starts so helpers don't repeat what's understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid opinion-based questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Math.SE is for logical/mathematical questions, not open-ended opinion polls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame questions so they have objective answers or well-defined criteria; avoid purely subjective 'what is better' questions without mathematical criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try to avoid duplicates and use system suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the suggested duplicate links and related-questions mechanisms to prevent reposting previously answered questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing a title the system suggests possible duplicates—inspect them in another tab. If none apply, proceed; otherwise edit to avoid duplication. Duplicate prevention keeps the repository useful and navigable.
